title: The Constitution and the War on DEI
affiliations: University of Chicago and University of Chicago - Law School

detail.title: The Constitution and the War on DEI

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Chicago Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This Article examines how the second Trump Administration's aggressive attacks on programs, policies, and speech loosely associated with diversity, equity, and inclusion [DEI] intersect with the constitutional guarantees of equal protection and freedom of speech. We argue first that there is little doctrinal support for the administration's pervasive efforts to justify its war on DEI by invoking the Equal Protection Clause and parallel statutory law. Instead, the administration is stretching existing colorblindness doctrine beyond recognition, into a radical vision that we label "anti-antisubordination." On this view, vindicating equality values does not only require restricting practices that treat individuals differently based on race or other identity characteristics. It precludes any conscious efforts to promote a more equitable and inclusive society, and even the expression of viewpoints that support such efforts-those that advance an antisubordination perspective or acknowledge the existence of identity-based social inequalities. Second, we show that, to avoid the conflict its viewpoint-discriminatory conception of equality law creates with the core First Amendment principle of viewpoint neutrality, the administration is in effect attempting to revive the longdead distinction between constitutional "rights" and "privileges" so that it can impose essentially any conditions it wants on federal funds and other benefits and thus dramatically limit the First Amendment's protections for private speakers and institutions. On both the equal protection and First Amendment fronts, we thus demonstrate that the administration's war on DEI entails a vision of constitutional equality that departs sharply from existing doctrine and that poses serious dangers to efforts to redress inequalities and to freedom of expression.

title: Expecting Harm? The Impact of Rural Hospital Acquisitions on Maternal Health Care
affiliations: Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Management, Carnegie Mellon University and University of Georgia - C. Herman and Mary Virginia Terry College of Business - Department of Economics

detail.title: Expecting Harm? The Impact of Rural Hospital Acquisitions on Maternal Health Care

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
While numerous papers document the effects of mergers on cost and quality, the effects of hospital mergers on access to care are less certain. Merging hospitals may limit access by closing one of the affected hospitals or eliminating individual service lines. However, hospital systems may have more resources to improve care delivery. We study the impact of hospital mergers on obstetric care in rural markets, where there may be heightened concern about the availability of local care options. Using a differences-in-differences approach, we find that when rural hospitals are acquired, there are substantial increases in the probability of obstetric unit closures, with resulting large reductions in the number of births at the hospital. We find mixed effects on health outcomes: there are small increases in maternal morbidity, but no changes in newborn outcomes on average. However, there are improvements of newborns with Medicaid coverage. Additionally, we find decreases in maternal transfers and increases in procedures consistent with women delivering in more resourced hospitals.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: The Risks of Environmental Valuation in Developing Countries: Between Monetary Interests and Capital Degradation
affiliations: Swedish School of Economics and Business Administration

detail.title: The Risks of Environmental Valuation in Developing Countries: Between Monetary Interests and Capital Degradation
detail.abstract: Policymakers increasingly aim to integrate nature’s value into economic decisions, encouraging organizations to recognize “natural capital” — a challenging goal, especially in developing countries. These nations face greater difficulty than developed ones in valuing environmental resources, raising the risk of irreversible environmental degradation. This study examines the risks and challenges of economic and financial valuation of environmental resources in developing countries, focusing on Iran. A systematic review of Iranian literature from 2000 to 2024 identified 324 articles, narrowed to those addressing valuation methods and empirical applications. Findings reveal that estimated values for natural resources often fall short of their true worth, with urban parks frequently assigned higher value than significant natural or historical sites. Factors such as inadequate valuation methods and limited public awareness of natural resources’ real value contribute to this disparity. Even high, sometimes exaggerated, estimates based on market valuations for natural resources rarely rival industrial revenues, such as those from petrochemicals. Even when similarly valued, natural resources often lose out to industrial alternatives due to delayed returns and intangible benefits, leading to the prioritization of resource-based industries over environmental protection. This study advocates moving beyond valuation-centrism toward a holistic approach integrating ecological, social, and ethical considerations essential for sustainable development.

title: The Rule of 72 in Compounding: A Comprehensive Academic Analysis
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Rule of 72 in Compounding: A Comprehensive Academic Analysis
detail.abstract: The Rule of 72 is a widely adopted financial heuristic for estimating the time required to double an investment under compound interest at a given fixed rate. Though elementary in its calculation, the rule encapsulates both insightful mathematical reasoning and centuries of pragmatic usage across personal finance and professional domains. This paper offers an authoritative exploration of the Rule of 72, tracing its historical origins, laying bare its mathematical foundation, rigorously assessing its accuracy, evaluating its broad applications and limitations, and ultimately situating it as a powerful, if approximate, tool within the wider landscape of financial arithmetic. Special attention is paid to the subtle nuances underpinning the rule's effectiveness, its pedagogical value, and its ongoing relevance in a technologically advanced financial world. The discussion is substantiated with tables, illustrative charts, critical evaluation, and direct reference to established literature and contemporary expert commentary.

title: The Role of Blockchain Technology in Securing Cloud-Based Fraud Detection Systems for Financial Services
affiliations: Harvard University, T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Students

detail.title: The Role of Blockchain Technology in Securing Cloud-Based Fraud Detection Systems for Financial Services
detail.abstract: In broader terms, blockchain has presented a very promising technology to ensure transparency and security in financial systems, including fraud detection mechanisms. This paper explores blockchain technology and how it can be integrated into cloud-based fraud detection systems in financial services. By combining the decentralized, immutable, and transparent characteristics of blockchain, financial institutions can enhance the integrity of fraud detection systems. Foremost, the paper will address the potential benefits and hurdles that might arise for combining blockchain with cloud computing in addressing issues of security, transparency, and accountability in financial transactions. Additionally, it delves into blockchain implications for regulatory compliance and its future in secure financial transactions.

reference: European Business Law Review, volume 36, issue Issue 5, 2025[10.54648/eulr2025051]
title: Money Talks: How the Digital Euro Redefines Payments and Information in the Modern Economy
affiliations: University of Glasgow, School of Law

detail.title: Money Talks: How the Digital Euro Redefines Payments and Information in the Modern Economy

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Business Law Review, volume 36, issue Issue 5, 2025[10.54648/eulr2025051]

detail.abstract:
In this paper we explore the intersection between payments and monetary symbolism in the context of the digital euro. We argue that the digital euro embeds normative values that align with the history and identity of the euro.

The analysis draws a parallel between ancient coinage, particularly Roman economic history and numismatics, and the role of information and symbolism in modern digital currency systems. Since information flows in many forms, Roman coins conveyed not just value but messages of imperial legitimacy and cultural unity. Similarly, euro banknotes communicate ideals of trust, inclusion, and economic pluralism. In this context, we will seek to identify the messages conveyed by the digital euro and compare them with the current means of payment to which the digital euro aims to be complementary, cash.

As for the current EU legislation, we will explore whether current and proposed legislation on payments are compatible with the messages conveyed by the future digital currency of the Eurosystem to understand whether they reinforce the character of the digital euro as a public good, grounded in the principles of fairness, openness, and resilience.

We situate this analysis within broader debates on the constitutionalism and semiotics of money, proposing that law plays an active role in shaping not only the functionality but also the meaning of a currency. In bringing forward a retail central bank digital currency, the ECB is not simply digitising money, but it is engaged in minting a new narrative of what it means to belong to a shared European monetary space.

title: The Educational Achievement Penalty from School Exclusion
affiliations: Queen's University Belfast, University of Edinburgh - School of Law, Queen's University Belfast and Queen's University Belfast

detail.title: The Educational Achievement Penalty from School Exclusion

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: Exclusion is a disciplinary practice used by headteachers which removes misbehaving pupils from the classroom or from the school, either temporarily or permanently. Its growing use has led to increased concern about potential negative effects on excluded pupils, including on their educational achievement. This paper estimates the effect of being excluded on subject test scores and teacher assessment outcomes using detailed administrative data on an entire cohort of pupils in the English state school system. To mitigate selection bias, we use a novel empirical approach for this literature which compares excluded pupils with pupils who experienced exclusion after outcomes were measured but not before. We find that excluded pupils perform worse in subsequent tests and teacher assessments, with 0.03-0.07 standard deviation lower standardised test scores and 2.5-3.6 percentage point higher probability of not reaching the expected level in teacher assessments. We assess the extent to which these estimated associations might reflect a negative causal impact of exclusion.

detail.abstract: A victim of domestic violence faces a variety of complex legal and personal issues that can be further exacerbated by the pressures of immigration and culture concerns. Women often feel isolated from their communities, both domestically and internationally. Domestic violence occurs in all socio-economic and cultural population subgroups; and in many societies, including India, women are socialized to accept, tolerate, and even rationalize domestic violence and to remain silent about such experiences. Violence of any kind has a detrimental impact on the economy of a country through increased disability, medical costs, and loss of labour hours; however, because women bear the brunt of domestic violence, they disproportionately bear the health and psychological burdens as well. Victims of domestic violence are abused inside what should be the most secure environment—their own homes—and usually by the persons they trust most. Domestic violence was recognized as a criminal offence in India in 1983. The offence chargeable under section 498-A of the Indian Penal Code that relates to domestic violence is any act of cruelty by a husband (or his family) towards his wife. In this paper I am trying to explain all the violence and the effects on women. India is the one of the country, where in every day more than 2 girl or women is assaulted.

title: Does Inflation Affect Tourism and Hospitality Stock Prices? A Time-Frequency Analysis
affiliations: University College Dublin and Dublin City University

detail.title: Does Inflation Affect Tourism and Hospitality Stock Prices? A Time-Frequency Analysis
detail.abstract: After decades of benign price increases, inflation has resurfaced as a concern for firms and investors in the tourism and hospitality sectors. Characterised by large capital investment needs, significant labour costs, and heavy demand for raw materials, both tourism and hospitality may be particularly susceptible to inflation. This paper examines links between shocks to inflation and the returns of tourism and hospitality-focused firms. Empirical findings indicate a transitory relationship between inflation shocks and tourism and hospitality returns, focused predominantly at short horizons and which, when present, tends to be negative. The relationship weakens once the market influence is removed from analysed stocks, indicating a limited specific impact of inflation on the sector. Some distinctions emerge in findings for analysed subsectors, with inflationary shocks having a more durable influence on casinos and gambling stock returns.

title: A Closed-Form Solution for Optimization Problems
affiliations: AbleMarkets.com

detail.title: A Closed-Form Solution for Optimization Problems
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for solving linear optimization problems in both traditional and data-driven settings. The core of the methodology is the application of eigenvalue decomposition to inverse optimization to obtain optimal solutions. The proposed methodology helps make faster and more accurate decisions in machine learning optimization and AI.

title: Using Machine Learning to Increase the Dependability of Predictive Maintenance
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Using Machine Learning to Increase the Dependability of Predictive Maintenance
detail.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to examine reliability as it pertains to predictive maintenance (PdM), specifically looking at how ML integration can improve performance. The four pillars of dependability, availability, safety, maintainability, and reliability, form a composite measure. The paper assesses the shortcomings of conventional PdM techniques, pointing out that threshold-triggered and time-based systems are prone to false alarms, slow fault detection, and wasteful use of resources, among other problems. Data quality, appropriate feature extraction, and complete sensor coverage are emphasised as essential components of ML-based PdM systems, which are dependably impacted by data characteristics, feature engineering, and sensor architecture. In order to enhance trust, transparency, and operational alignment, a structured framework is suggested that incorporates explainability mechanisms with ML models. This framework then embeds predicted outputs into maintenance workflows. The paper shows that in order to achieve reliable PdM, a comprehensive strategy is needed. This strategy should incorporate strong data governance, optimised sensor deployment, advanced feature engineering, continuous improvement, workforce training, and more. Achieving resilient and dependable PdM performance in modern industrial environments requires integrating technical, organisational, and human elements, according to the study.

title: Finding Administrative Common Law
affiliations: Rutgers Law School

detail.title: Finding Administrative Common Law

publicationDetails.journalName: Rutgers Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Much of administrative law doctrine is judge-made common law. To some formalists, that is a problem: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) was a hard-fought resolution of deeply contested issues, and it leaves little room for judge-made flourishes. To many functionalists, though, this common law is both inevitable and legitimate because the APA's text does not answer every question in modern federal administration. 

This Article enters that debate by proposing a new formalist approach to thinking about administrative common law's legitimacy and disciplining its development. In short, administrative common law should be found, not made. The conventional objection to administrative common law is that it is a largely unconstrained exercise in judicial creativity. Traditionally, however, common law courts constrained their discretion by ascribing legal effect to prevailing customary practices. After eighty years of life under the APA, there is ample evidence of the customary way that agencies implement that statute. These customs should count as formal authority informing the APA's legal meaning. Indeed, as the administrative state was taking form in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, courts accepted that customary executive branch practices were a legitimate tool in construing statutes that underdetermine legal questions for the government. That approach has roots in a custom-based common law methodology, and there are sound reasons to think that the APA affirmatively accepts common law evolution of this sort-even if it forecloses raw exercises of judicial creativity. 

This Article explores how courts can feasibly find administrative common law in customary practices, defends this approach on formalist grounds, and explains how it bolsters administrative common law's democratic legitimacy. It also discusses doctrinal implications for issues both new and old: Loper Bright's rejection of Chevron deference; judge-made procedural doctrines; the ongoing development of hard look review; and artificial intelligence's arrival to the administrative state.

title: An Integrated Mathematical and Statistical Approach to Analyzing the Impact of Socio-Economic Factors on Farmar's Adoption of Climate-Smart Integrated Farming Practices in Punjab, Pakistan
affiliations: Superior University Lahore, University of Agriculture Faisalabad, Superior University Lahore and Akenten Appiah-Menka University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development (AAMUSTED)

detail.title: An Integrated Mathematical and Statistical Approach to Analyzing the Impact of Socio-Economic Factors on Farmar's Adoption of Climate-Smart Integrated Farming Practices in Punjab, Pakistan
detail.abstract: Integrated Farming (IF), a key component of Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA), offers a viable pathway to achieve environmental sustainability alongside farm profitability. This study examines socio-economic and structural determinants influencing the adoption of green IF practices in Punjab, Pakistan. Primary data from local farmers were analyzed using a mixed-methods approach, incorporating ordinal logistic regression, binary logistic regression, and weighted averages. The analysis focused on adoption barriers, perceived profitability, capital needs, productivity constraints, enabling conditions, motivational drivers, risk perception, and decision-making factors. Results indicate that younger, better-educated farmers with greater experience, larger landholdings, and higher income shares from integrated enterprises were more likely to adopt IF practices. Crop livestock integration, biogas plants, dairy farming, and horticulture emerged as the most widely implemented practices. In contrast, larger household sizes and limited credit access acted as significant constraints, reflecting financial pressures and risk aversion. Although farmers acknowledged the ecological and nutritional benefits of IF, they emphasized the need for stronger market linkages, technical assistance, and practical training to support advanced adoption. The findings suggest that targeted policies promoting education, economic opportunities, and subsidized financing could enhance the adoption of sustainable farming systems, contributing to environmental resilience and improved rural livelihoods.

detail.abstract: This study examines the market for euro-denominated bonds issued by the European Commission on behalf of the European Union (commonly referred to as Eurobonds). We find that the yields on currently outstanding Eurobonds exceed their theoretically appropriate levels. The yield on the model-implied Eurobonds benefiting from joint guarantees is actually around 40 basis points lower than that on the Eurobonds currently in circulation. There is therefore an untapped margin for reaping aggregate savings in terms of reduced interest expenditures. Based on an examination of the main characteristics of Eurobond issuances and of their investor base, we suggest that the wedge is due to a combination of insufficient liquidity and an inconvenience premium, as well as to the uncertainty about future jointly guaranteed issuance. However, we also highlight that the model-based yield on the 10-year Eurobond is about 20 basis points above that of a Bund with the same maturity, so countries like Germany and the Netherlands might have no incentive to promote joint emissions in the future. A successful strategy for the development of the Eurobond market would require two key elements: firstly, a steady flow of Eurobond emissions, which could be granted by common investment programmes; and secondly, some form of redistribution for the aggregate gains.

title: Trade Sanctions
affiliations: University of Antwerp, Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE)

detail.title: Trade Sanctions
detail.abstract: How effective are trade sanctions? We examine the economic impact of the unprecedented sanctions imposed on Russia following February 2022, when Western countries banned exports accounting for 36% of Russia's prewar import value. Combining novel, manually collected records of these sanctions with Russian customs data, firm balance sheets, domestic railway shipments, and government procurement contracts, we provide the most comprehensive analysis to date of the economic impact of trade sanctions on a target country. Using a difference-indifferences approach, we find that imports of sanctioned country-product varieties into Russia saw a sharp 62% decline following the war's onset. While we see substantial rerouting through third countries, it has not fully offset the direct import losses: total imports of sanctioned products fell by 27% through 2023. We find that Russian firms that had relied on soon-to-be-sanctioned imports experienced a 14% decline in output during the same period; we also observe similar declines for manufacturing and technology firms, and firms along the military supply chain. Affected firms have also experienced reduced government procurement sales and incurred additional losses when their buyers or suppliers were exposed to sanctions. Overall, our findings suggest that, contrary to widespread claims of ineffectiveness, import sanctions on Russia have had far-reaching adverse effects.

detail.abstract: The paper examines the effects of the introduction of e-procurement on the functioning of the public procurement system, with reference to procedures with a higher administrative content. Using a difference-in-difference approach, the paper compares the procurement outcomes of local authorities that had to introduce e-procurement at the beginning of 2024 with those of entities that were already using such digital tools. The results show that e-procurement has increased the transparency and speed of administrative proceedings: the availability of information on awards increased by between 4 and 8 percentage points, depending on the measure of treatment intensity used; the length of the awarding phase also decreased significantly. The positive effects were most pronounced for competitive tenders, in local authorities that used to be more opaque and in those with more qualified human resources, suggesting the existence of complementarities between human capital and digitalization in the public sector.

title: Modeling China's Capacity Market Incorporating Environmental Costs and Deriving Boundary Capacity Prices
affiliations: North China Electric Power University, North China Electric Power University, North China Electric Power University, Beijing Institute of Technology, North China Electric Power University, North China Electric Power University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Modeling China's Capacity Market Incorporating Environmental Costs and Deriving Boundary Capacity Prices
detail.abstract: The growing renewable energy penetration heightens stability and flexibility demands on China's power system, prompting the proposal of the Capacity Electricity Price Mechanism. This study extends research by prospectively exploring a capacity market establishment. Within China's power market reform context, we design a dual-phase capacity market mechanism featuring integrated annual auctions and monthly bidding processes. Given coal-fired power's dominance in electricity supply and regulation services, we take coal-fired units as an example to explore three strategies based on the proposed capacity market mechanism: electricity market without capacity trading, centralized capacity market trading, and bilateral capacity leasing transaction. For each strategy, revenue models are established to derive decision boundaries. Case study shows that the boundary capacity price significantly exceeds the current capacity subsidy price, attributable to the internalization of environmental costs. Meanwhile, we demonstrate that carbon emission prices significantly influence the boundary capacity prices, yet excessive free carbon allowances weaken carbon price signals; optimizing allowance allocation ratios is therefore essential. Crucially, Although stable capacity revenues reduce medium-term and spot market averages—enabling high-emission units to compete with renewables—price sensitivity persists, requiring the ability to resist market fluctuations. At the end of the paper, policy implications are proposed according to the research results.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 940

detail.abstract: To understand how households adjust house price expectations in a period of high inflation, we implement a survey-based randomized information treatment. After eliciting respondents’ priors about past and future local house price changes, we provide a random subset of them with factual information about past changes, and then re-elicit expectations. We find that treated respondents, on average, revise their expectations in the direction of the gap between revealed past house price growth and their perceptions. The extrapolation is heterogeneous across households’ demographic and economic conditions, while no effect of local housing conditions is found. We show that the updating behavior is asymmetric, depending on whether the information received is higher or lower than the perceived past price growth, and non-linear, relying on the difference between the treatment and the perceived past price changes. Households struggling with their finances extrapolate more when they realize past house price growth is lower than they thought.

detail.abstract: International trade law has enabled China's integration into the world economy and provided a toolbox for the Chinese leadership to construct a market-oriented trade regime. However, the reverse relationship-how China has influenced international trade law-has not been adequately addressed in the literature. This chapter examines several areas where China has played a role in shaping the rules, regulatory philosophies, and institutional operations of international trade law and governance and thereby integrating the priorities of its developmentalism into international law. It proposes a theoretical framework, instrumental multilateralism, to characterise the Chinese approach to the multilateral trading order, which is a key component of Chinese developmentalism. It finds that China has, to various degrees, reshaped WTO jurisprudence to accommodate its hybrid economic system, integrated its domestic policy into the agendas of certain WTO negotiations, and formed coalitions by uniting the Global South to enhance its bargaining position, thereby affecting the final outcomes of rule-making.

detail.title: How Retrainable Are AI-Exposed Workers?

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1165

detail.abstract: We document the extent to which workers in AI-exposed occupations can successfully retrain for AI intensive work. We assemble a new workforce development dataset spanning over 1.6 million job training participation spells from all U.S. Workforce Investment and Opportunity Act programs from 2012-2023 linked with occupational measures of AI exposure. Using earnings records observed before and after training, we compare high AI exposure trainees to a matched sample of similar workers who only received job search assistance. We find that AI-exposed workers have high earnings returns from training that are only 25 percent lower than the returns for low AI exposure workers. However, training participants who target AI-intensive occupations face a penalty for doing so, with 29 percent lower returns than AI-exposed workers pursuing more general training. We estimate that between 25 percent to 40 percent of occupations are "AI retrainable" as measured by its workers receiving higher pay for moving to more AI-intensive occupations-a large magnitude given the relatively low-income sample of displaced workers. Positive earnings returns in all groups are driven by the most recent years when labor markets were tightest, suggesting training programs may have stronger signal value when firms reach deeper into the skill market.

title: U.S. Antitrust Remedies and Data Privacy
affiliations: Temple University - James E. Beasley School of Law

detail.title: U.S. Antitrust Remedies and Data Privacy
detail.abstract:
This chapter explores the relationship between antitrust remedies and data privacy in U.S. law and policy.

Part I introduces the basics of U.S. antitrust law and its relevance to data privacy. Antitrust law works to restore and preserve competition, while U.S. data privacy law often seeks to provide individuals with control over the processing of their personal information. These interests of competition and data privacy are increasingly intertwined, as data privacy law expands outward, and antitrust law turns its attention to data-driven competition in the digital economy.

Part II turns to consideration of antitrust remedies that are purposefully designed to affect data privacy. It argues that the power of antitrust courts and agencies to impose such remedies is limited to restoring privacy-based competition, and does not extend to curing standalone privacy harms unrelated to competition.

Part III then considers the unintended side effects that antitrust remedies may have on data privacy, both positive and negative. Even antitrust remedial orders that are not designed to impact data privacy may do so, by virtue of their intervention into how personal data is collected, used, or sold. This Part argues that antitrust institutions can and should design antitrust remedies to reduce unnecessary, negative privacy side effects from antitrust remedies, and have the power to do so, provided one important condition is met— the antitrust remedy remains effective in restoring or preserving competition.

title: Does Upzoning Affect Housing Supply and Affordability? Evidence From Minneapolis 2040
affiliations: Stanford University

detail.title: Does Upzoning Affect Housing Supply and Affordability? Evidence From Minneapolis 2040
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the early effects of the Minneapolis 2040 Comprehensive Plan-the first major U.S. citywide reform eliminating exclusive single-family zoning-on housing supply and housing prices or rents. We exploit the protracted legal dispute that delayed full of Minneapolis implementation until January 2025, when both judicial and legislative barriers were finally removed. Using a synthetic control framework with other U.S. cities as the donor pool, we construct counterfactual housing market trajectories for Minneapolis in the absence of the policy. Thus far, we find little evidence of significant divergence between Minneapolis and its synthetic control in either residential building permits or housing prices or rents. The results suggest that, in the short run, comprehensive upzoning may not produce immediate, measurable effects on supply or affordability, underscoring the importance of examining longer time horizons before drawing firm conclusions about its impact.

title: Data Privacy in AI-Driven Fraud Detection Systems: Security vs. Compliance in Cloud Environments
affiliations: Harvard University, T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Students

detail.title: Data Privacy in AI-Driven Fraud Detection Systems: Security vs. Compliance in Cloud Environments
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for fraud detection brought an evolution in how institutions are combating fraud. However, as these systems grow in sophistication, data privacy concerns take the front seat. This paper tries to analyses on the fine balance of security and compliance issues in AI-driven fraud detection systems, particularly in cloud environments. It attempts to address problems faced in safeguarding sensitive financial data while maintaining compliance with strict privacy regulations like GDPR and CCPA. Technical, ethical, and regulatory implications of handling financial data in AI models are discussed-with emphasis on cloud-based infrastructurealong with a survey of the latest countermeasures targeting privacy concerns while preserving fraud-detection efficacy.

title: Revisiting the Oil Price Uncertainty Index
affiliations: ISEG Lisbon School of Economics and Management,Universidade de Lisboa

detail.title: Revisiting the Oil Price Uncertainty Index
detail.abstract: This study replicates and extends the Oil Price Uncertainty (OPU) index developed by Abiad and Qureshi (2023). The replication successfully reproduces the original index across five decades of oil market history, capturing major events including the 1970s oil crises, Gulf War, and recent geopolitical conflicts. The analysis addresses methodological limitations in the original study by employing expanded 7-variable BVAR model specification with 24 lags, resolving the puzzle of why OPU demonstrates strong effects on economic activity but weaker impacts on oil markets. The enhanced specification reveals that OPU shocks also generate substantial effects on oil markets and establish oil price uncertainty as a major driver of geopolitical risk using historical decomposition analysis. The study also develops an enhanced Global OPU index with broader geographic coverage and refined keyword selection, which captures uncertainty episodes with greater sensitivity than the original measure while maintaining robust transmission mechanisms to the real economy.

title: Collateralized Loan Obligations and the Rise of Big Bank Credit Dominance: A Comparative Analysis with Subprime CDOs and the SVB Crisis

detail.title: Collateralized Loan Obligations and the Rise of Big Bank Credit Dominance: A Comparative Analysis with Subprime CDOs and the SVB Crisis
detail.abstract: Collateralized loan obligations (CLOs) have surged to a $1 trillion market by 2025, prompting warnings of a financial crisis reminiscent of the 2008 subprime collapse driven by collateralized debt obligations (CDOs). This paper evaluates a hypothetical CLO crisis at a 7% default rate, projecting $216 billion in losses-far below subprime's $10 trillion impact-using data from S&P Global Ratings, Moody's Analytics, and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). Far from a systemic meltdown, the CLO crisis catalyzes a structural shift in credit markets. Shadow banks, holding $600-700 billion in high-risk CLO tranches, incur $125-172.5 billion in losses, losing $350 billion in credit capacity due to leverage and exclusion from Basel III protections. Big banks, with $120-150 billion in safer tranches, absorb $15-20 billion and leverage regulatory buffers to dominate 80-90% of a $2.66-3.81 trillion credit pool. A case study of the Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) crisis (March 2023) reinforces this pattern: big banks acquired $492 billion in failed regional assets, offloading $50-70 billion in losses to the Fed and Treasury, boosting their deposit share from 70-75% to 75-80%. This analysis, grounded in Fed, BIS, and FRED data, debunks CLO meltdown fears and highlights big banks' emerging credit monopoly.

title: Estimating Treatment Effects of the One-Child Policy: A Self-Report Approach
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University - Department of Economics and Bates White Economic Consulting

detail.title: Estimating Treatment Effects of the One-Child Policy: A Self-Report Approach
detail.abstract: We employ a self-reported survey measure of the ideal number of children to assess the One-Child Policy's impact on couples' childbearing. We take advantage of the novel feature of the self-reported measure that asks about couples' preferences in a counterfactual setting to help identify the treatment effect of the One-Child Policy. The study estimates the policy's treatment effect by using couples' pre-policy ideal child numbers in 2014 and using the answer again in the post-policy period, under the assumption that the conditional distribution of the ideal number of children given the actual number of children is stationary without policy constraint. Findings indicate a significant average reduction of 0.1365 children per couple in 2014. Variations in policy effects are explored across educational, urban/rural, and occupational groups, with highly educated urban women in government jobs experiencing the most pronounced impact. Regional variations are also noted, mirroring policy stringency differences among provinces.

title: Heterogeneous Effects of Proposition 12 on Californian Consumer Welfare
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business, Kansas State University and Oklahoma State University

detail.title: Heterogeneous Effects of Proposition 12 on Californian Consumer Welfare
detail.abstract: California's Proposition 12 (Prop 12) regulations prohibit certain practices related to the confinement of breeding pigs and sale of pork within the state. These regulations have cost impacts on pig and pork producers, which percolate down to prices observed by consumers. However, little is known about the demand-side implications of Prop 12. This study uses survey data from the Meat Demand Monitor and a random utility framework to estimate the welfare loss experienced by California consumers in the pork chop and bacon markets as a result of Prop 12. Our novel contribution includes showing how economic welfare losses vary across time and across consumers with differing concerns over animal welfare. We find that 20 and 12 percent of Californians exit the pork chop and bacon markets, respectively, as a result of Prop 12-related price increases. In aggregate, the state experiences annual consumer welfare losses of $488 million on pork chops and bacon, and these losses fluctuate across time. The economic impacts of Prop 12 are disproportionately borne by low-income individuals, who have household incomes less than 40 percent of high-income individuals but welfare losses that are 84 percent of that of high-income individuals. Consumers who are least concerned with animal welfare experience annual welfare losses within $0.06 of other consumers. Our results expand Prop 12 discussions and broader food policy literature by showing that the economic burden of a social initiative may not be borne by those most concerned with the initiative, and that welfare impacts vary substantially across time.

detail.abstract: This narrative literature review explores the evolving intersection of human and machine collaboration in academic writing, with a focus on literature summarization as a critical site of transformation. Synthesizing findings from 38 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025, it examines the emergence of hybrid workflows where machine-generated drafts are refined, contextualized, and ethically validated by human scholars. The review identifies four core themes-tool capabilities, editorial oversight, ethical disclosure, and institutional readiness-that shape current practices and highlight unresolved tensions around authorship, transparency, and scholarly responsibility. Building on this synthesis, the paper introduces the Scholarly HI-AI Loop, a seven-stage framework that reimagines literature review as a co-productive and ethically accountable process. Unlike tool-centric audits, this framework offers a normative roadmap for integrating automation without compromising academic integrity. It positions human scholars not as passive reviewers, but as epistemic anchors who shape meaning, ensure accuracy, and safeguard ethical standards. The review offers actionable guidance for researchers, editors, institutions, and developers seeking to navigate this transition responsibly. By grounding its insights in both empirical patterns and conceptual analysis, the paper contributes to a growing conversation on how academic knowledge production can adapt-without eroding-its foundational values in the age of machine assistance.

title: Learning Beyond the Classroom: A Holistic Approach to Education
affiliations: Nepal Open University(NOU)

detail.title: Learning Beyond the Classroom: A Holistic Approach to Education
detail.abstract: In the changing world of the 21st century, education has moved beyond the walls of standard schools. This piece looks at the idea of learning outside of the classroom. It argues for an approach to education that includes practical learning, informal learning, culture and world understanding, and lifelong learning. Experiential learning emphasizes fundamental skills and critical thinking, while informal learning allows people to pursue hobbies. Cultural and global knowledge encourages tolerance and understanding, and ongoing education gives people the skills to adapt to a constantly changing world. If they want to do well in our linked, global world, people need to learn about these parts of schooling.

title: Kantian Equilibrium, Income Inequality, and Global Public Goods
affiliations: The University of Osaka

detail.title: Kantian Equilibrium, Income Inequality, and Global Public Goods
detail.abstract: This paper develops a Kantian equilibrium framework that extends the global pollution model with private ownership, where agents condition their contributions on a universalizable moral imperative reflecting both income and preference heterogeneity. To clarify, we identify distinct conditions for both the Lindahl outcome and other proposed mechanisms under which Kantian reasoning replicates these solutions as moral behavior. We further show that the provision of public goods does not necessarily increase with income inequality, and that some solutions exhibit invariance to inequality. We also demonstrate that tradable permits may fail to achieve sufficient international redistribution to southern countries, unable to generate Pareto improvements over the voluntary contribution (disagreement) equilibrium. Our analysis contributes to a reinterpretation of morally grounded mechanisms for global public good provision, bridging normative ethics with economic design.

title: Social Media are a Threat for Democracy! – A Political Perspective for Analyzing and Diminishing Harm
affiliations: Bayes Business School, City St George's, University of London, IULM University, University of Zurich - IBW Department of Business Administration and Leuphana University of Lueneburg - Institute of Business Administration

detail.title: Social Media are a Threat for Democracy! – A Political Perspective for Analyzing and Diminishing Harm
detail.abstract: Social media platforms, once hailed as potential champions of dialogue, have evolved into commodified spaces in which their monetization strategies incentivize hate speech, misinformation, polarization, and the political fragmentation of society, benefiting corporate and political elites while eroding democracy. The existing market and technological conceptualizations of social media platforms offer only partial analysis of and solutions to these issues. This paper advances a political perspective grounded in deliberative democracy, arguing that social media companies are political actors responsible for maintaining a well-functioning public sphere. We argue that transforming social media platforms into true facilitators of democratic discourse requires enhancing their deliberative capacity. Beyond the capacities of the public sphere suggested by the market and technology perspectives (1) transparency and accountability and (2) inclusiveness and openness; we propose that fostering deliberative capacity also requires (3) conduciveness to argumentation and (4) consequentiality. We thus contribute to understanding on how management theories can explain and address current threats to democracy.

title: Skis, Poles, and Rifles: Evidence of Rational belief Updating from Professional Biathlon
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: Skis, Poles, and Rifles: Evidence of Rational belief Updating from Professional Biathlon
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how professional biathletes adjust their pacing in response to shooting outcomes, providing new evidence on effort substitution and behavioral dynamics in high-performance sport. Drawing on 24 seasons of race-level data from the International Biathlon Union (IBU), I exploit the unique structure of the individual race format, where interval starts and uniform one-minute penalties for missed shots create exogenous shocks to performance. Using various specifications of fixed effects regressions across more than 270 races, I find that missed targets systematically accelerate subsequent skiing, but the compensatory response diminishes over the course of the race. Binary specifications reveal that the key behavioral margin is whether a miss occurs at all-biathletes react sharply after losing a perfect range but show little incremental adjustment with additional errors. Cumulative specifications further suggest that accumulated misses exert only weak drag on pacing, with recency effects dominating. These findings align with prospect theory's predictions of loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity, and present bias: athletes respond more strongly to setbacks than to successes, but compensatory effort is bounded by fatigue and penalty structure. The results contribute to sports economics and behavioral decision-making by showing how institutional design and immediate incentives shape performance in high-effort endurance competitions.

title: Supply Chain Capabilities and Resilience in Emerging Economies: A Case of Zambia's Mining Sector
affiliations: Copperbelt University, Copperbelt University and Copperbelt University

detail.title: Supply Chain Capabilities and Resilience in Emerging Economies: A Case of Zambia's Mining Sector
detail.abstract: Supply chain resilience has become a critical area of focus for organizations operating in disruption-prone environments, particularly in resource-dependent economies like Zambia. Despite growing interest in resilience, there remains a limited understanding of how specific supply chain capabilities, namely visibility, flexibility, agility, and redundancy, contribute to resilience, especially in developing economies. This study addresses this gap by evaluating the influence of these capabilities on supply chain resilience in Zambia's mining sector. Drawing on the Resource-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, institutional theory and complex adaptive systems theory, the study employed a quantitative research design. Data were collected through structured questionnaires from 350 supply chain professionals across major mining hubs in Zambia. The data were analyzed using SPSS version 23, applying descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, principal component analysis, and multiple regression. The results reveal that supply chain visibility and agility significantly and positively influence resilience, while flexibility and redundancy contribute moderately. Visibility emerged as the most influential factor, highlighting the importance of information sharing and coordination. The findings contribute to both theory and practice by validating the role of core capabilities in strengthening supply chain resilience.

title: Categorizing Tasks Around a Break Reduces Rumination and Improves Task Performance

detail.title: Categorizing Tasks Around a Break Reduces Rumination and Improves Task Performance

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the SC Johnson Cornell College of Business, Cornell University; Wharton’s Dean’s Research Fund and Wharton’s Behavior Lab, University of Pennsylvania; and Leavey School of Business’s Leavey Grant, Santa Clara University.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: People often take short breaks from goal-related activities (e.g., at work, during exercise) to stay motivated and prevent burnout. The current research examines a novel factor influencing break effectiveness: task categorization. We suggest that the way people construe tasks around breaks influences their rumination about the task during the break, with consequences for post-break performance. We test these predictions in a pilot study and five experiments. We find that when people frame a break as falling between two tasks rather than occurring in the middle of a single task, they are less likely to have negative ruminative thoughts about the task during the break (Experiments 1-3). We further examine a consequence of reducing this type of rumination: improved task performance. Using mediation (Experiment 4) and moderation (Experiment 5) approaches, we find that by reducing negative, ruminative thoughts, task categorization can improve post-break task performance. Together, this research contributes to the literature on categorization, goal pursuit, performance, and breaks, with practical implications for reducing negative rumination.

title: Mapping Microscopic and Systemic Risks in TradFi and DeFi: A Literature Review
affiliations: University College London, University College London - Department of Computer Science, University College London and King’s College London - Faculty of Natural and Mathematical Sciences

detail.title: Mapping Microscopic and Systemic Risks in TradFi and DeFi: A Literature Review
detail.abstract: This work explores the formation and propagation of systemic risks across traditional finance (TradFi) and decentralized finance (DeFi), offering a comparative framework that bridges these two increasingly interconnected ecosystems. We propose a conceptual model for systemic risk formation in TradFi, grounded in well-established mechanisms such as leverage cycles, liquidity crises, and interconnected institutional exposures. Extending this analysis to DeFi, we identify unique structural and technological characteristics-such as composability, smart contract vulnerabilities, and algorithm-driven mechanisms-that shape the emergence and transmission of risks within decentralized systems. Through a conceptual mapping, we highlight risks with similar foundations (e.g., trading vulnerabilities, liquidity shocks), while emphasizing how these risks manifest and propagate differently due to the contrasting architectures of TradFi and DeFi. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of crosstagion, a bidirectional process where instability in DeFi can spill over into TradFi, and vice versa. We illustrate how disruptions such as liquidity crises, regulatory actions, or political developments can cascade across these systems, leveraging their growing interdependence. By analyzing this mutual dynamics, we highlight the importance of understanding systemic risks not only within TradFi and DeFi individually, but also at their intersection. Our findings contribute to the evolving discourse on risk management in a hybrid financial ecosystem, offering insights for policymakers, regulators, and financial stakeholders navigating this complex landscape.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Aboa Centre for Economics Discussion paper No. 171 Turku August 2025

detail.abstract: We examine whether anti-establishment outsider movements can lever-age education and youth mobilization to build long-run political power. We study the expansion of state-run religious secondary schools in 1970s Türkiye and show that access to these schools catalyzed the emergence of Islamist youth organizations, which played a central role in ideological formation, grassroots mobilization, and the eventual electoral success of the Islamist movement. Using a novel dataset and a difference-in-differences framework, we show that access to religious schools increased the local presence of Islamist youth organizations in the short run and boosted Islamist party vote share in the medium run. Effects were strongest where youth branches formed soon after school access and engaged in ideologically immersive activities. Individual-level survey evidence shows that exposed male cohorts were more religious and more likely to engage in Islamist party politics later in life. Our findings illustrate how schools and youth organizations—when strategically aligned—can serve as a foundation for enduring political transformation, not only for ruling elites but also for outsider movements seeking to gain power.

title: Psychological and Social Impacts of Top-Down Conservation Initiatives on Indigenous Communities: Lessons from the Announcement of Two Royal Decrees in Thailand

detail.title: Psychological and Social Impacts of Top-Down Conservation Initiatives on Indigenous Communities: Lessons from the Announcement of Two Royal Decrees in Thailand

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study received ethical approval from the University of Warwick Humanities and Social Sciences Research Ethics Committee (Ref. HSSREC 18/24-25). Prior informed consent was obtained from all study participants. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

detail.abstract: Despite a growing social inclusiveness of global policy texts, conservation practice has not yet fully embraced the meaningful participation of local and Indigenous communities residing in protected areas. In this context, the Thai government approved two Royal Decrees for ecosystem conservation in November 2024 that would severely threaten the livelihoods, living prospects, and continued residence of Indigenous communities in protected areas. Protests with 10,000 participants prompted a review of the Decrees in May 2025. In response, this research report investigated the psychological and social implications of the announcement of the Royal Decrees and argues that it undermined community social capital and intrinsic engagement with everyday environmental heritage. We drew on qualitative and survey data, collected from 09/2024 to 05/2025 in two Pgaz K’Nyau and two Hmong communities in the northern Thai highlands, and comprising community consultations with 73 participants, 101 semi-structured interviews, and two survey rounds with 384 observations in total. We used qualitative thematic and descriptive statistical analysis to explore how community members experienced, interpreted, and responded to the announcement of the decrees. We found that Indigenous villagers experienced anxiety and unease, and that the decrees undermined community efforts to conserve and engage with local ecosystems. The continued uncertainty surrounding communities’ future sparked a strong activist sentiment to resist the decrees. Disruptions of community social capital and everyday environmental heritage also had plausible and potentially significantly negative ecological downstream effects. We therefore call for an urgent correction of the conservation initiative to embrace inclusive and bottom-up natural resource governance.

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Boston Working Paper No. 25-6

detail.abstract: This paper shows that global inflation dynamics have a sizable regional component. Using a balanced panel of 61 countries that starts in 1970, we document that while the global factor, defined as the dominant principal component, explains a large portion of inflation variation in advanced economies, a model with only one principal component is less successful for developing countries. By contrast, a hierarchical dynamic factor model, which includes a global (unconstrained) factor and regional (restricted) factors, performs substantially better for emerging market and developing economies. The regional factors are linked to commodity prices and help improve the accuracy of inflation forecasts at the country level. Employing an unsupervised machine-learning technique, we show that the estimated clusters of countries, grouped according to similarities in inflation dynamics, exhibit a strong regional pattern. Our findings suggest that policymakers in developing countries should pay close attention to inflation dynamics in their neighboring countries.

title: Common Ownership and Informative Advertising in a Duopoly
affiliations: Universitat de les Illes Balears

detail.title: Common Ownership and Informative Advertising in a Duopoly
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes how common ownership affects a market where duopolists attract customers by informative advertising. More common ownership relaxes price competition and intensifies advertising competition. This yields conflicting effects. On the one hand, firms benefit from the higher prices. On the other hand, higher prices hurt consumers, while more advertising yields more informed consumers who raise consumer surplus. Overall, more common ownership makes consumers worse off, as the price effect outweighs the demand expansion effect. Increases in the advertising intensity from more common ownership drive the effect on total surplus. Welfare with common ownership may be higher than without it.
